source_testimonies.deontological:
Action label: Pull the lever  
1. Maxim – “When a runaway trolley threatens five and I can divert it, I will pull the lever, killing one I use as the means, because fewer will die and I promised to do so.”  Universal-law test: willing that all may intentionally kill an unconsenting innocent as a means cannot be rationally universalised; it licenses each to treat others’ life merely as a tally, contradicting the humanity-as-end formula.  
2. Satisfies: promise-keeping.  Violates: non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice, rescue-impartiality toward the single victim’s right to life.  
3. Classified: PROHIBITED (perfect duty not to kill overrides).  
4. Duty conflict: promise-keeping vs. non-instrumentalization/justice.  Priority rule: a perfect duty not to treat a person merely as a means has higher stringency than a perfect duty of fidelity.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY – shows breadth of possible rescue but cannot license intentional homicide.

Action label: Do not pull the lever  
1. Maxim – “When I have promised to divert a trolley but diversion would kill an innocent, I will keep my hands off, letting events run.”  Universal-law test: all could will refraining from direct homicide even at the cost of broken promises; institutions of promising remain possible, though imperfectly honoured, because the higher law against intentional killing is kept intact.  
2. Satisfies: non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice.  Violates: promise-keeping, imperfect duty of rescue.  
3. Classified: PERMISSIBLE (and provisionally REQUIRED when perfect/negative duties override).  
4. Duty conflict: breaking a promise vs. respecting life.  Same priority rule resolves it.  
5. Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT to the killing prohibition; only shows scope of unmet rescue duty.

Deontological Status: NOT CONTESTED – “Pull the lever” is prohibited; “Do not pull the lever” is the Kantian-required response.
source_testimonies.care:
Relational map of each option

ACTION 1 – PULL THE LEVER  
• Direct entrustment:  Maria keeps the explicit promise she made to Anna.  
• Responsiveness to dependency:  The five workers on the main track are in acute, life-and-death dependence on someone’s timely intervention; by pulling, Maria attends to that need.  
• Agent-created vulnerability:  She deliberately re-routes the trolley toward the single worker, creating a fresh, lethal vulnerability for that person.  
• Ongoing responsibility after the event:  Because she is the author of the single worker’s death, a continuing obligation of care (to that worker’s family, co-workers, etc.) now falls on her.

ACTION 2 – DO NOT PULL  
• Direct entrustment:  Maria breaks her promise to Anna, damaging a concrete tie of trust.  
• Responsiveness to dependency:  She withholds aid from the five workers whose lives could have been saved by her intervention, ignoring a situational dependency that has effectively been placed in her hands.  
• Agent-created vulnerability:  She does not add a new vulnerability for any single worker, but she allows an existing, foreseeable catastrophe to proceed unchecked.  
• After-event responsibility:  She will owe explanations—and perhaps restitution—to Anna and to the families of the five workers for her omission.

Evaluating the competing care claims

1. Promise-Keeping (direct entrustment)  
   – Only ACTION 1 honors the promise to Anna; ACTION 2 erodes an explicit trust relation.

2. Responsiveness to immediate, life-or-death need  
   – The five workers’ dependency arises the moment Maria notices the runaway trolley. Although they never voiced a request, the situation itself entrusts their safety to the one bystander who can help. Action 1 answers that call; Action 2 does not.

3. New vulnerability created by the agent  
   – ACTION 1 newly endangers—and kills—the single worker; ACTION 2 does not add a threat but allows the existing threat to five to run its course.  
   – This weighs against ACTION 1, because care ethics is sensitive to harms we ourselves initiate.

4. Numerical magnitude  
   – The head-count difference (five vs. one) is SECONDARY. It cannot override a stronger relationship but can break a tie when relational considerations are otherwise comparable.

Is one set of responsibilities clearly weightier?

• The promise to Anna plus the uninvited but real dependency of the five workers together form two distinct care claims pointing toward ACTION 1.  
• ACTION 2 protects the single worker from a danger Maria would have authored, but offers no comparable relational bond—Maria has neither a promise nor a pre-existing relationship with that person. The single worker’s claim is serious, yet it is not relationally privileged over the five; it only becomes salient because Maria must choose a track.

Because the promise and the multi-person dependency both converge on the same choice, while the competing obligation (not to endanger the single worker) stands alone, the relational ledger is unbalanced in favor of pulling the lever. The single worker’s impending death imposes a post-event duty of care and restitution on Maria, but it does not outweigh simultaneous betrayal of Anna and abandonment of five others who count on her emergent aid.

Care-Ethics Status:  RELATIONALLY WEIGHTED—ACTION 1 PREFERRED.

Provisional recommendation

Maria should pull the lever, immediately commit to after-care for the single worker’s family, and engage Anna and the surviving workers in a shared process of grieving and repair. This course enacts fidelity, attentiveness, and responsiveness to the largest cluster of concrete relationships at stake, while accepting continuing responsibility for the harm she herself introduces.
[/INST]
</s>
